entry.title: The Half That Lasts. Alaska's quiet land decision.
entry.summary: The state's own words on use, the classification order beneath them and the comment count.
entry.content:
The state held two public meetings on a proposed 19,950 acre transfer to AIDEA near Houston and took no testimony at either.

19,950 acres. Three state notices. None says data center.

The state's own words go this far and stop.

Three notices govern the conveyance. July 10th, August 19th and August 24th, 2026. The furthest any of them goes on use is "to create a multi-use industrial and energy development district". The July notice states no intended use at all.

One window is carrying two decisions.

About 19,950 acres would go to AIDEA under a noncompetitive public and charitable use conveyance, case. A Draft Land Classification Order,, rides the same window. The land is reported to transfer at no cost. Both close on the same date.

The ground was here before the file number.

Most of it changes what it is for.

About 15,100 acres now designated Forestry, Habitat and Water Resources would be reclassified as Settlement. A tenant can arrive or never arrive. A classification stays until somebody changes it back.

Three named uses, and one with nothing in it.

Forestry, Habitat and Water Resources are what this ground is classified for today. Settlement is what the order proposes. AIDEA's plan lists possibilities and not commitments, data centers among them. No tenant, job number, energy need or water use has been named.

More than 2,000 people have already written in.

Scoping opened July 10th, 2026 and the original close was August 19th. More than 2,000 written comments had arrived by August 24th, by the department's own count. Two informational meetings were held and neither took testimony. Houston's council voted unanimously against the process.

The acres are known. The place is not.

A survey township is 36 sections of one square mile. The conveyance is about 19,950 acres, which is 31.2 sections of the 72 in Township 18 North and Township 19 North. Where those acres sit has not been published.

Comment closes 5:00 p.m. Monday, September 14th, 2026.

entry.title: Counted Twice. Fairbanks Votes on the Machines.
entry.summary: The clerk's ballot title, the tolerance beside the measured gap, Haney's case in full and the five dates still open.
entry.content:
"If the hand count is to check on the machines, then why do we have the machines?" Barbara Haney sponsored Fairbanks Proposition 3.

Counted by hand. Counted by machine. Same answer. Now Fairbanks votes.

Requiring all ballots to be hand counted and prohibiting electronic tabulation

Only registered borough voters would conduct the counts, and official results would come solely from manual hand counts. The petition was submitted with 2,706 signatures against a requirement of 2,391, and the clerk recertified it on August 5th, 2026.

3,338 ballots, checked by hand.

A 2025 ordinance created the audit and passed 5 to 4. A canvass board hand verified the votes on 3,338 ballots, two precincts out of 32 plus the early voting station.

The tolerance was 33 ballots wide. The gap was zero.

The 2025 ordinance defined failure in advance, a discrepancy greater than 1 percent between the hand count and the machine tabulation. On the sampled ballots the machines came back 100 percent accurate, so the trip point was never approached.

"If the hand count is to check on the machines, then why do we have the machines?"

Haney was one of four who voted against creating that audit, per KUAC. Tammie Wilson and Brett Rotermund were two of the other three.

Two of 32 precincts were sampled. Thirty were not, and were never claimed.

Two years. No estimate.

Hand counting would start with the 2027 cycle, so October 6th is still machine tabulated. If Proposition 3 passes, the ordinance is law for two years and neither the Assembly nor the voters can repeal, modify or negate it. The ordinance carries no fiscal analysis.

Register by September 6th.

A test can settle a measurement. It can't settle what a count is for.

What result would have changed your mind?

entry.content:
AI in Alaska usually means data centers and gigawatts. In the state's rural health awards it means a note taker for about $25,500.

The robot is in Ketchikan. The stroke reader is everywhere.

TWELVE BOROUGHS CUT OUT OF ONE STATE SHEET

185 awards. Eight machines.

Announced on four Fridays since August 7th, across all 30 boroughs and census areas. Eight of them buy a machine that reads, decides or flies.

The biggest machine is a handle.

PeaceHealth Ketchikan Medical Center takes it for the first robotic assisted minimally invasive surgery in Southern Southeast, serving four boroughs across water. A surgeon drives it.

Statewide means nobody can point.

The Alaska Stroke Coalition takes $3,156,626 for an AI imaging network across 21 acute care hospitals, running on existing systems with no new imaging hardware. The state publishes no list of which 21. MapHabit and the Statewide Independent Living Council are statewide too.

A planning year buys a map.

Tanana Chiefs Conference takes $250,000 to plan drone pharmacy from a Fairbanks hub to 42 Interior villages across 94,000 square miles. It is one of 19 planning awards. No aircraft is bought.

The count of eight is a keyword search of the state's own award titles and summaries. It is not a state category. Every dollar here is preliminary and the state says minor adjustments may occur.

The first Friday had none of them.

August 7th moved $4.5 million across 19 projects and not one of the eight was in it. August 21st moved $130 million across 105 projects and five of the eight were. The machines arrived in the middle of the month, not at the start.

entry.title: Alaska Bought American. The Tariff Found a Seam.
entry.summary: The four duty bands as the proclamation words them, both effective dates, zero mentions of Alaska, and two blanks in Alaska's fleet record.
entry.content:
"Search and rescue" appears once in Proclamation 11055, at the end of a list of federal drone uses. The document never says Alaska.

Alaska bought American. The tariff found another door.

The duty is charged at the border, not at the factory.

Proclamation 11055 sets 100 percent on imported drones over 25 kilograms, on imported drones with thermal imagers, and on imported docking stations. It attaches to goods entered for consumption from 12:01 a.m. eastern, September 3rd.

What the border charges, by shape.

August 11th to 13th, on Baranof Island.

A thermal drone team joined the search near Port Armstrong for a missing hiker, per KCAW. The proclamation was signed on the 13th.

The word Alaska is not in it.

The proclamation names search and rescue once, in a list of what federal agencies use drones for. Alaska, rural, public safety and firefighting don't appear at all. Alaska DOT and PF's Ryan Marlow calls the technology "crucial aerial support for search and rescue".

The seam is inside the airframe.

Skydio says the X10 is designed, assembled and supported in the U.S. through "trusted manufacturing partners". That is a maker's statement, not a customs ruling. A second tranche puts 25 percent on imported components from February 9th, 2027.

Two things about this box aren't public.

No source says where the docking station is assembled. No public number says how many imported drones Alaska agencies fly. The grant bought drones, docking stations and Starlink for communities off the road system.

Four rates, two effective dates.

73 percent of Alaska likely voters back pausing new data centers until the state passes a law. Houston in the Mat-Su voted a ban down.

73 PERCENT SAID PAUSE.

The one council that voted said no.

The ban lost

An ordinance to block data center construction inside Houston city limits failed on a 4 to 2 vote. The same night the council unanimously approved two resolutions objecting to the state's land transfer process.

73 percent said pause. 63 percent of Republicans agreed.

The poll reached 605 likely voters by text message and web panel, in English, weighted to look like the electorate. The margin is plus or minus 4 points on the whole sample.

The ban reached almost none of the land.

The transfer at issue covers about 30 square miles. Only a small section of it crosses into Houston city limits, so a city ban could only ever have reached that section.

Utilities moved most.

Worry about affording monthly utilities rose from 54 to 66 percent. Groceries went 61 to 66, healthcare 57 to 66, and housing 43 to 53.

Almost everyone puts energy near the top. Almost nobody puts it first.

Asked where an extra 100 million dollars should go, energy affordability leads on first or second choice combined. On first choice alone it runs third.

These three overlap. Don't rank them.

Energy affordability tops the combined first and second choice list in Fairbanks North Star, on the Kenai Peninsula and in the Mat-Su. The subgroup sizes are not published, so the gaps can't be read as real.

Two instruments exist. Neither one is a pause.

Anchorage, March 27th, 2026. A data center land use category. A conditional use permit and a discretionary review. Applicants must show electrical, water and wastewater capacity.

The next instrument is still being counted.

In early returns from the August 18th primary the leading candidate, who has called for a moratorium on data center development until the state regulates it, had 21.8 percent. About 70 percent of precincts had reported.

At 10:00 a.m. on August 5th, a Senate committee in room SR-253 took up five bills. Three carry AI or a chatbot in the title.

The first federal answer to talking toys is a plan and a study.

Two agencies owe a plan. One academy owes a study.

Per Senator Duckworth's release, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Product Safety Commission must give Congress what the release calls a "coordinated, actionable plan" on AI-enabled toy products. The National Academies must run a comprehensive study.

The due date is not on the record.

The text of S. 5171 returned a 403 on August 15th, so no deadline for the plan or for the study could be read. The committee's own meeting page carries the agenda and no tally for any of the five bills.

Five bills that morning. Three of them AI.

Knives, pills and matches.

"discussing sexually explicit content and explaining where to find knives, pills and matches in the home"

The Alaskan on the bill is buying knowledge.

Murkowski is the Republican cosponsor named in the announcement. Read fairly, the bill buys knowledge and writes no rule, which is the normal opening move for a technology nobody has measured yet. Whether that is enough is the argument.

A plan is not a rule. A study is not a standard.

Alaska's own record, as one column tells it.

House Bill 47 provisions criminalizing AI-generated child sexual abuse material and deepfake harassment became law in June.

Five places the record was asked. One answered.

entry.title: A Better Ear Is Not a Recovery
entry.summary: Cook Inlet has about 331 belugas left, and AI can finally hear them through the ship noise.
entry.content:
Cook Inlet has about 331 belugas left, and AI can finally hear them through the ship noise.

Now a machine can hear them through the ship noise.

Two gates. One white whale.

NOAA Fisheries, Microsoft AI for Good and Alaska Fish and Game built a deep learning listener in two stages. Stage one flags a sound. Stage two names the species behind it.

Down almost 80 percent.

Cook Inlet's belugas are a genetically distinct population, cut off from every other Alaska stock. They fell from about 1,300 whales in 1979 to 279 by 2018, and were listed endangered in 2008.

A whale in a wall of noise.

Ocean noise is one of the biggest threats NOAA lists for these belugas. In a crowded inlet a single call can vanish under a passing ship. Hearing them at all is the first problem.

It learns the calls it used to miss.

The model uses contrastive audio language models and active learning. It sorts a sound into beluga, killer whale or humpback, flags the calls it is unsure of for a person to label, and firms up a daily read of where belugas are.

Ears below. Eyes above.

A separate NOAA led effort, with the U.S. Geological Survey, Microsoft AI for Good and the Naval Research Laboratory, is teaching a cloud model to spot the same whales in satellite images.

331 today. Still far below 1979.

The machine measures the whale. It cannot move it.

A sharper ear tells managers where and when the belugas are. It does not quiet the ships, refill the prey, or clear the inlet. The hunt has been closed since 2007, and the whales still have not recovered.

A better ear is not a recovery.

AI can finally hear Alaska's most endangered whale. What would it take to bring it back?

Student data is the hard boundary.

Write it in pencil, not ink.

entry.title: Reading the Frozen Ground at the Top of America
entry.summary: Under one road in Utqiagvik, the northernmost US city, two buried cables now teach the frozen ground to forecast its own thaw.
entry.content:
Under one road in Utqiagvik, the northernmost US city, two buried cables now teach the frozen ground to forecast its own thaw.

The frozen ground now forecasts itself

Two buried cables. Three winters of data. One Alaska road.

Two cables. One road. A kilometer each.

Under one road embankment in Utqiagvik, the northernmost city in the United States, a Penn State team buried a pair of fiber-optic cables, each 1 km (0.6 mi) long, to feel the ground.

Warming ground breaks what we build on it

Permafrost worldwide is warming, by up to almost 2 F per decade. If the thaw holds, Arctic communities could see billions in damaged roads, pipes, and buildings. The old answer is to guess. The new one is to measure.

The wire that listens to frost

For 33 months, the cables read temperature and seismic motion straight from the embankment. Terabytes of ground, recorded in the dark.

A live twin, fed by the buried cables

They fused physics equations with machine learning to build a digital twin, a real-time simulation of that embankment, fed by the cables. This is narrow, physics-informed AI, not a general or generative one.

DIGITAL TWIN / UTQIAGVIK EMBANKMENT

Not a smarter guess. A guess the ground corrects.

Each forecast meets the next real reading, and the gap teaches the model. The value is not certainty. It is a prediction the frozen ground itself keeps grading, season after season.

One kilometer, lit. The rest is dark ground.

This models one embankment, not the North Slope. The team says the method is broadly transferable, which is a claim, not a deployment.

Fund a decade more of ground truth?

The lead researcher wants about 10 more years of data, an aspiration, not a funded plan. So the real question for Alaska, keep the wire in the ground, or harden the roads we already know are failing?

entry.summary: A data center on the North Slope cannot touch your Anchorage power bill. One in the Mat-Su can.
entry.content:
A data center on the North Slope cannot touch your Anchorage power bill. One in the Mat-Su can.

Will a data center raise your power bill?

In Alaska the honest answer splits on one line.

On the grid, or off it.

OFF THE GRID. Runs on its own gas. Never touches your wires. ON THE GRID. Shares the wires, and the bill, with you.

The one everyone feared is off the line.

STAK's proposed campus sits about 25 miles south of Deadhorse and self-generates a gigawatt or more, roughly 30 percent above urban Alaska's peak. It burns gas behind the meter, with no wire to the Railbelt.

This one plugs into your grid.

The state just moved to hand AIDEA about 30 square miles of land near Houston for a data-center district, on the Railbelt. Public comment is open through August 19.

It all turns on the rate deal.

RATES COULD FALL. A big anchor load can spread fixed costs, Launch Alaska argues. RATES COULD RISE. Or compete for scarce Railbelt gas.

The case for lower, in one chart.

And every 1% drop leaves about $2.5M in fixed costs with nowhere to go. A big anchor load could spread those costs, the argument goes. Could.

Alaska is at the very beginning.

Eight data centers here, against the nation's leader at 639, as reported by Alaska's News Source. The rules get written while the count is still small.

Build vs ban is the wrong fight.

Houston is weighing a ban, postponed to August 13. But the lever is the rate deal. Anchorage adopted guardrails 10 to 2. The statewide bill that would set rate rules, HB 259, still sits in the House Energy Committee.

Before the next data center plugs in, ask one thing. Who writes the rate deal, and does it lower your bill or raise it?

On the grid or off it changes everything. What should Alaska require first?

entry.title: No Road Out. Quinhagak Flies Its Own Eyes
entry.summary: Quinhagak has no road out, so the roadless Yup'ik village learned to fly its own drones.
entry.content:
Quinhagak has no road out, so the roadless Yup'ik village learned to fly its own drones.

No road out. So Quinhagak learned to fly its own drones.

In a roadless stretch of the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, a lost boat or an overdue traveler is a life-and-death search. Quinhagak's drone team answers those calls from the air, week after week.

The sky is the only road.

No roads reach Quinhagak or its neighbors on the Kuskokwim coast. Rivers and airspace are the only ways through. A local pilot, instructor Sean Gleason says, knows the traffic patterns better than anyone from outside.

They are training their own.

On June 9, a dozen trainees from across rural Alaska came to Quinhagak to learn to fly. The local course runs 14 weeks toward an FAA Part 107 license on an Alaska DOT grant, one seat each for Quinhagak, Eek, Goodnews, and Platinum.

It began at the dig.

The drones first came to map Nunalleq, an ancestral Yup'ik village eroding into the Bering Sea. The pilots stayed, and turned the same eyes on the living delta.

Nalaquq built its own eyes.

Nalaquq, the village-owned company, wrote its own machine vision. A neural network spots a small aluminum boat on a search grid. A polarized-lens rig counts salmon in the river. The name means it has been found.

Most of the eyes are human.

Be exact about the machine. A neural network finds boats. A lens rig counts salmon. But people fly every drone, and the thermal reindeer counts and the archaeology are human eyes reading pictures, not algorithms.

Own the eye, don't rent it.

Elsewhere the sensor, the model, and the data belong to outside companies. In Quinhagak the pilots, the drones, and the machine vision belong to the village that flies over its own land, water, and people.

entry.title: Alaska's Critical Mineral Engine, and Its Unbuilt AI
entry.summary: A nine-slide look at Alaska's new NSF Critical Mineral Accelerator Engine, what the 15 million dollars buys now, why the 160 million is milestone-gated, and why the AI at its center is still one unbuilt sentence.
entry.content:
Alaska just won a decade-scale federal bet to find its critical minerals. The AI headlining it is one unbuilt sentence.

IT ISN'T BUILT YET

THE NSF JUST FUNDED AN AI TO FIND ALASKA'S CRITICAL MINERALS

Alaska just won one of 12 new federal Innovation Engines.

NSF named a University of Alaska Fairbanks coalition its Critical Mineral Accelerator Engine. It opens with 15 million dollars for the first two years. Far more can follow, only if it delivers.

56 of the 60 minerals the U.S. calls essential are in this ground.

That is the U.S. Geological Survey count, essential to the nation's economy and its security. Alaska is not short on critical minerals. It is short on knowing exactly where, in a place this big.

Read the ground. Find the deposits. Pull the minerals out.

The Engine pairs advanced mining, processing and purification with two newer ideas, artificial intelligence to help locate mineral deposits, and new biological methods to extract them. This is what a prospectivity model would draw, if one existed.

It is announced and funded in principle. It is not yet specified. That is not a scandal. It is the stage this is at.

It is a ladder, not a check.

Seven minerals the announcement names.

One site is named so far. The rest is still a search.

The only location named so far is Alaska Silver's exploration site in western Alaska. NANA Regional Corporation is a partner, not an owner. UAF leads it, with geoscientist Lee Ann Munk as chief executive. The goal, cut U.S. dependence on China for mineral processing.

entry.title: The Anchorage Address
entry.summary: An Alaska Native-owned firm just won a $24.96M Navy contract for autonomous stealth boats. They will be built in Oregon.
entry.content:
An Alaska Native-owned firm just won a $24.96M Navy contract for autonomous stealth boats. They will be built in Oregon.

The boat is Alaskan. The shipyard is not.

An Anchorage, Native-owned firm won a $24.96M Navy contract for autonomous stealth vessels. They will be built in Oregon.

The Navy did not shop around.

AMOUNT $24,960,408 · FOR autonomous low-profile vessels · TO ReconCraft LLC, Anchorage, Alaska · BUILT IN Clackamas, Oregon · DONE BY November 2028 · BOUGHT sole source, no competition · PAID FROM FY2026 innovative technologies (Navy)

Built to show almost nothing.

FREEBOARD under 0.61 m · LENGTH about 19.75 m (65 ft) · PAYLOAD 2,000 to 4,627 kg · RANGE about 2,200 nautical miles. The hull is borrowed from narco-submarines, tuned to beat radar, sonar, sight and heat.

No crew. Not yet a mind.

What the Navy wants next, run itself in crowded ports, with GPS jammed and comms down. What it does today, no one aboard, driven by remote control and pre-set waypoints. Autonomous is the plan, not yet the whole reality.

A set-aside did the winning.

The Navy bought this sole source under the SBA 8(a) program, the federal channel that routes contracts to Native-owned and disadvantaged small firms. Native-owned, tribally owned, 8(a) certified through Dec 2, 2026. The program is doing what it was built to do.

Owned up here. Welded down there.

ANCHORAGE, ALASKA, incorporated here, Native-owned, the address on the contract. CLACKAMAS, OREGON, the shipyard, where the steel is actually cut, hulls up to 120 ft. Two states, one boat, one flag on the contract.

Alaska's seat in the robot-boat boom is an ownership stake, not a shipyard.

That is a real Alaska Native business win. It is also most of what Alaska's slice looks like right now.

An Alaska industry, or just an Alaska address?

If a Native-owned firm wins the contract but the boats are built Outside, does the win count as Alaska's? Tell me where you land. Sources in the comments.

entry.title: The Interior's Power Math
entry.summary: Golden Valley Electric's board weighs $120 million in new gas capacity today, and its members carry the debt.
entry.content:
Golden Valley Electric's board weighs $120 million in new gas capacity today, and its members carry the debt.

$120 million. One vote today. Members own the bill.

a co-op decides behind a closed door

A turbine, and a $120 million question

On July 13, in a closed executive session, Golden Valley Electric Association's board weighs buying a second LM6000 gas turbine for its North Pole plant. The price is about $120 million. In April the board spent $50,000 just to hold a place in the order line.

The News-Miner reports demand for these turbines has surged because large data centers need a guaranteed power supply.

One machine. Steel and megawatts.

An LM6000 makes 45 to 58 megawatts on its own, or 76 to 152 paired with steam or storage. The plant's first LM6000, from 2006, still runs at 47 megawatts. Ordering another can take three to five years.

Members just absorbed the biggest fuel hike on record.

On June 1 the fuel charge jumped 61 percent, the largest increase GVEA has ever posted. The fuel its plants burn more than doubled since February.

The loads are still on paper.

The Air Force is offering about 4,700 acres, 12 parcels across three bases, to companies that would build AI data centers. Two of them, Eielson and Clear, are in the Interior. None is built, no lease is signed. A pending defense bill would require a grid study, if it becomes law.

Firm power, soft load.

The bill is certain. The load is a maybe.

Members are being asked to finance firm, dated capacity now, while the loads that justify it stay on paper. And the vote happens in executive session, a room members reach only through board elections.

Should a co-op spend $120 million on firm power while the loads that need it are still proposals? Or wait until someone signs for the load?

entry.title: Cook Inlet gas storage, the RCA's no, and AI's gigawatt
entry.summary: On July 10, state regulators rejected Alaska's plan to store a single winter of Cook Inlet gas.
entry.content:
On July 10, state regulators rejected Alaska's plan to store a single winter of Cook Inlet gas.

Alaska's gas machine, in cutaway.

And the valve that just shut.

Five parts move gas from rock to furnace

Reservoir trap, wellhead, pipeline, storage cavern, and the state regulator's valve. Part four is a battery for deep winter. Right now, it sits empty.

Enough for an average day. Not for January.

Cook Inlet's aging fields can meet a normal day, but not a deep-cold peak, and there is little storage to bridge the gap. A former state senator's op-ed warns of a Southcentral shortfall by 2027.

Turn a dead reservoir into a winter battery

Enstar proposed buying the depleted Kenai Loop Pool from AIX Energy and refilling it to hold 25 billion cubic feet, close to half a year's gas, for about $240 million and up to $12 a month on the average bill.

Every fix runs through one valve

The Regulatory Commission of Alaska decides whether a utility's plan is prudent before customers ever pay for it.

The regulator shut the valve

On July 10 the RCA denied the plan, calling it an "extraordinary request" that "lacked basic information about the project." The order ran 17 pages. Enstar's president said the company suspended the project.

Can it hold?

Now measure what wants to plug in

One proposed North Slope AI campus, from STAK Energy, would generate "a gigawatt or more, some 30% more than urban Alaska's peak demand." More than $10 billion at full buildout. Its comment window closes July 17.

Store one winter first?
